en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Gabbhinīvagga 66.
The Second Training Rule Concerning a Married Woman:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunīs were ordaining women who had reached twelve years of age and had married, but who had not trained for two years in the six rules.
They were foolish and incompetent, and did not know what was allowable or what was unallowable.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as above] ...were indignant, complained, and grumbled:
“How can these bhikkhunīs give the full admission to a married girl who is twelve years old but has not trained for two years in the six rules?
… [The Buddha asked: “Is it true, monks, that bhikkhunīs are giving the full admission to a married girl who is twelve years old but has not trained for two years in the six rules?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can these bhikkhunīs give the full admission to a married girl who is twelve years old but has not trained for two years in the six rules?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of those with faith…” [and so on].
Having rebuked them and given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to grant formal permission for training in the six rules for two years to a married woman who has reached full twelve years of age.
And this, bhikkhus, is how it should be granted.”

When she has completed twelve years as a married woman, she should approach the Saṅgha, arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the bhikkhunīs, sit down on her haunches, raise her joined palms, and speak thus:
“Venerable ladies, I, so-and-so, having completed twelve years as a married woman under Venerable so-and-so, request from the Saṅgha permission to train in the six rules for two years.
She should request a second time as well.
A third time she should be asked.
An experienced and competent bhikkhunī should inform the Saṅgha:
“Let the noble Saṅgha listen to me.
This woman, [name], having reached full twelve years of age and being a married woman, requests from the Saṅgha permission to train in the six rules for two years.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant permission to [name], who has reached full twelve years of age and is a married woman, to train in the six rules for two years.
This is the motion.
"Let the noble Saṅgha hear me.
This woman named so-and-so, who has been married for twelve full years, requests from the noble Saṅgha permission to train in the six rules for two years under the noble lady named so-and-so.
The Saṅgha grants permission to train in the six rules for two years to this woman named so-and-so, who has been married for twelve full years."

Whichever noble lady approves of granting the authorization for training in the six rules for two years to the woman named so-and-so, who is full twelve years of age and has been married, let her remain silent;
whichever does not approve, let her speak.
The Sangha has granted the authorization for training in the six rules for two years to the woman named so-and-so, who is full twelve years of age and has been married.
“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
She, having reached twelve years of age while still married, should be told:
“I undertake the undertaking of abstaining from taking life for two years without transgression... [and so on] ...”
“I undertake the training rule of abstaining from eating at improper times for two years, without transgressing this commitment.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked those bhikkhunīs in many ways for being difficult to support...
[and so on] ...and furthermore, bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whatever nun should give the full admission to a married girl who is more than twelve years old, but who has not trained for two years in the six rules, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so on].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"One who has completed twelve years" means:
"Having reached twelve years.
"One who has gone to a householder" means one who has gone over to another man.
"Two years" means two full years.
"One who has not trained in the training" means:
Either the training has not been given, or the training that was given has been violated.
"Should ordain" means she should confer full admission.
If, thinking “I will give the full admission,” she seeks out a group, a preceptor, a bowl, or a robe; or if she demarcates a boundary, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For the motion (ñatti), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For two proclamations (kammavācā), there are offenses of wrong-doing.
At the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā), there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the preceptor;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the assembly and for the teacher.
If she causes [a girl] to go forth through a legitimate legal act while perceiving it as a legitimate legal act, there is an offense of expiation.
If she gives the full admission while the legal procedure is legitimate, but she is in doubt about it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she gives the full admission while the legal procedure is legitimate, but she perceives it as illegitimate, there is an offense of expiation.
If she gives the full admission while the legal procedure is illegitimate, but she perceives it as legitimate, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If she gives the full admission while in doubt that it is an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she gives the full admission perceiving an illegitimate legal procedure as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense:
If she ordains one who has reached twelve years of age, is married, and has trained for two years in the six rules—
provided she is insane or is the first offender— [there is no offense].
The sixth training rule is finished.
